Brooklyn prosecutors and the FBI have seized or disrupted 241 websites and 112 servers tied to a crypto investment scam that allegedly stole tens of millions of dollars from Russian-speaking victims in the U.S.
The operation, carried out last week, came after a three-year investigation into a fraud network that relied on online infrastructure and IP addresses in Ukraine and other Eastern European countries, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said . No arrests were announced.
The scammers drew victims through Russian-language Facebook ads that promised investment opportunities. Fake advisers then called the victims and coached them to buy cryptocurrency and send it to fraudulent trading platforms.
When victims tried to withdraw their funds, the platforms locked their accounts or demanded more payments for supposed taxes and fees.
The scammers then “tried to exploit them again with false promises to recover their money,” Gonzalez said. Recovered data showed they contacted victims a few weeks after the initial fraud, offering to retrieve the stolen funds.
The DA’s Virtual Currency Unit had previously seized or disrupted 400 domains tied to crypto investment fraud, but replacement sites kept appearing.
This time, investigators targeted the servers, hosted by Eastern European and U.S. companies, that held victim data and the software used to run the fraud. The goal was to stop the operators from quickly launching new sites.
The case comes as crypto investment scams accounted for roughly 84% of the $8.65 billion in investment-fraud losses reported to the FBI in 2025, according to the bureau’s annual report .
Across all internet-crime categories, crypto-linked losses totaled $11.37 billion, approximately 54% of the $20.88 billion overall. Both percentages are calculated from the FBI’s totals.
Brooklyn authorities have seized about $300,000 and are working to recover more. Prosecutors said some victims lost their entire life savings.

The FBI has helped take down a crypto scam network that targeted Russian-speaking individuals living in the US and likely stole tens of millions of dollars.
The operation, described as “one of the biggest operational cyber disruptions undertaken by a local prosecutor’s office,” was led by Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez’s Virtual Currency Unit (VCU).
Russian-speaking people living in Brooklyn were targeted by crypto scammers operating a phony forex investment site that promised substantial returns via Russian-tailored ads.

Individuals were contacted by fake investment advisors and convinced into depositing funds on their supposed investment site.
Victims were shown fake gains, and when they tried to withdraw their funds, they were told their account was locked or that they had to pay more money to access it. 
Authorities dismantled 241 crypto scam domains and 112 servers across Ukraine, Eastern Europe, and America.
The group would also revisit individuals it had already scammed, luring them with recovery operations that promised to restore their stolen crypto.
Gonzalez’s local office was able to seize $300,000, but despite this, many Individuals lost their life savings.

(ASIC/Media) Summary Show Australia’s financial regulator proposed standards requiring cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset custodians to safeguard customer funds, ensure transparent trading and meet financial requirements. The rules take effect April 8, 2027, and existing firms may continue operating if they apply for a license by Oct. 7, 2027, while regulators review their applications. Australia's financial regulator proposed new standards for cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset custodians, setting out how companies must protect customer funds, execute trades and meet financial requirements under laws that take effect next year.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said it opened a consultation on the rules on Thursday, which would require affected firms to obtain or update their regulatory approval or license. The consultation closes on Nov. 27, with final guidance and standards expected in March 2027.
The proposals mark the next step in Australia’s effort to bring crypto businesses under the same regulatory framework as traditional financial firms. Parliament passed the legislation in April, joining jurisdictions such as the European Union, Singapore and Hong Kong, which have introduced dedicated crypto regulations.
Australia's move comes years after the 2022 collapse of FTX left about 30,000 Australian customers unable to access their money. Three years earlier, Cryptopia, an exchange in neighboring New Zealand , went bankrupt after a major hack.
The rules take effect on April 8, 2027. Crypto firms already operating in the country have until Oct. 7 of the next year to apply for a license and can continue doing business while ASIC reviews their applications.
For Australian investors, the changes would mean clearer rules on how exchanges hold their assets, execute orders and handle conflicts of interest. Crypto companies would face new compliance obligations and financial requirements to operate legally in the country.
"Our approach is based on the principle of 'same activity, same risk, same regulatory outcome' to align Australia with the approach of comparable overseas jurisdictions," ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland said.
Under the consultation paper , platforms would be subject to standards covering the separation and safeguarding of customer assets, trading transparency, settlement procedures and financial resources. The proposed trading rules also address market manipulation, conflicts of interest and how exchanges handle customer orders.
ASIC said it has recorded more than 140 applications from businesses seeking authorization to provide digital asset-related financial services. It also said stablecoins used for payments are being addressed separately through Australia's payment services reforms.

Russians have a little over eight months left to trade Bitcoin and other crypto directly with each other. From July 1, 2027, peer-to-peer deals—where two people swap rubles for coins without a regulated middleman—will no longer be legal, the Bank of Russia confirmed this week.
The clarification sits in updated guidance the regulator posted on its official website on October 12.
The legal basis is Federal Law No. 282-FZ , “On Digital Currencies and Digital Rights,” which President Vladimir Putin signed on August 4 and which took effect September 1. Article 30 lists the crypto operations residents may carry out without a licensed intermediary, and from July 2027 that list no longer includes trades between individuals.
From that date, residents may only trade crypto through, or directly with, companies that “organize the circulation” of digital currencies—mainly brokers licensed by the Bank of Russia and crypto exchange organizations listed in its registry.
The regulator also says individuals cannot move crypto from a digital account to their own non-custodial wallet, meaning a wallet where the owner holds the private keys instead of a company. Transfers from one person to another through addresses run by a digital depository—a licensed firm that records who owns which coins—are off the table too, even to settle a trade between them.
Lending crypto is also off-limits for ordinary users: only brokers, trustees, exchange organizations, and clearing houses can act as the lender in a crypto loan.
Since Binance sold its Russian business to CommEX in 2023, a standard way for Russians to get stablecoins has been peer to peer: the buyer wires rubles to a seller’s bank card and receives USDT, a dollar-pegged token, in return. That model is exactly what the new rules end.
From July 1, 2027, Russian banks will have to refuse clients who try to fund crypto wallets on foreign platforms, and won’t be able to accept rubles cashed out from those platforms, Andrei Tugarin, managing partner at GMT Legal, told Kommersant FM .

(Pincasso/Shutterstock) Summary Show Nearly $483 million in bitcoin and ether futures positions were liquidated over 24 hours as uncertainty about the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision weighed on cryptocurrency markets. Ether traders bore the brunt of the sell-off, with about $286 million in liquidations as ether fell more than 6 percent to roughly $2,350. Bitcoin declined about 3 percent to around $81,000, while losses spread to smaller tokens including Solana, dogecoin and Zcash. Nearly $483 million in bitcoin and ether futures positions were closed over the past 24 hours as cryptocurrency prices fell Thursday, with ether traders taking the largest hit.
Crypto losses worsened on Thursday morning as uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision weighed on markets. Bitcoin traded around $81,000, down roughly 3% over 24 hours, while ether lost more than 6% to about $2,350. XRP and Solana’s SOL fell around 5%, and dogecoin dropped roughly 6%.
Ether contracts accounted for about $286 million of liquidations, compared with $197 million for bitcoin, according to CoinGlass data checked during Asian morning hours. Ether fell about 6.4% to $2,356, while bitcoin lost roughly 3.2% to trade around $81,000.
Liquidations happen when traders use borrowed money and a price move leaves them without enough collateral to keep their bets open. The exchange closes the position automatically. Someone using $1,000 to control a $10,000 position, for example, can lose their backing on a move of less than 10% against them.
Those closures can add pressure to a falling market, forcing traders out regardless of whether they wanted to sell at that price.
Ether’s damage was larger even though its futures market is considerably smaller.
Outstanding ether contracts totaled about $30 billion, against $52 billion for bitcoin. The liquidation figures measure the value of positions closed, rather than the cash traders personally lost.
The selling reached smaller tokens too. Solana futures recorded about $31 million in liquidations as SOL fell roughly 5.5%. Zcash contracts added nearly $19 million, with ZEC dropping about 13%.
